question: What actually harms the body in an electric shock?
options: The voltage, on its own
The current flowing through the body, pushed by the voltage
The colour of the wire
The magnetism around the wire
explanation: Current through nerves, muscles and the heart does the harm. The voltage matters because it is what pushes that current through you.

question: Is it safe to touch both ends of an AA cell with dry fingers?
options: Yes: the push is too gentle to drive a harmful current through dry skin
No: any battery can give a deadly shock
Only if you wear gloves
Only for a few seconds
explanation: Dry skin is a good barrier, and a small battery's push is far too gentle to get through it. You will not even feel it.

question: Why is shorting a small battery dangerous even though it cannot shock you?
options: It makes the battery's voltage much higher
It sends electrons into the air
A huge current flows and the battery's energy turns into heat very quickly
It is not dangerous at all
explanation: In a short nothing limits the current except the battery itself, so all its power becomes heat. Batteries can burn skin, start fires or, for lithium cells, catch fire.

question: Why is the wall socket dangerous when small batteries are not?
options: Wall sockets contain more electrons
Its push is strong enough to break through skin and drive a dangerous current through the body
Wall sockets are always shorted
It is only dangerous in wet weather
explanation: The mains push can force its way through even dry skin, and its alternating current is especially good at disturbing the heart. Never touch it.

question: A device has been unplugged from the wall for a minute. Is it safe to open?
options: Yes, as soon as it is unplugged
Yes, if it is switched off
Only if it is cold
No: capacitors inside can still hold a dangerous charge, and this course never opens mains devices
explanation: Capacitors store charge and can keep it long after unplugging. Never open anything that plugs into the wall.

question: Something in your circuit starts to smell and smoke. What do you do first?
options: Disconnect the battery or power, then think
Grab the hot part and pull it out
Blow on it to cool it down
Add another battery to see what happens
explanation: Disconnect first, think later. A hot part stays hot for a while, so do not grab it.

question: Which statement about a car battery is correct?
options: It can give a deadly shock through dry skin
It is safe in every way
It is safe to touch, but a short across its terminals can make metal glow and burn you
It has a higher voltage than a wall socket
explanation: Its push is low, so touching it is safe, but it can deliver an enormous current into a short. Safe to touch is not the same as safe to short.
